stories.title: Cascadia, 1700
stories.text: The catalog gives it one nominal point off the coast, {lat}° N {lonW}° W, magnitude {mag} ({magType}), with no depth. USGS on the Japanese records of its tsunami: “Some noted that no parent earthquake had been felt; they were wondering what had set off the waves. They had no way knowing that the tsunami had been spawned during an earthquake along the coast of northwestern North America.”

stories.title: New Madrid, 1811–12
stories.text: The catalog lists {n7} earthquakes of magnitude {seven} or more between {boxS} and {boxN}° N, {boxW} and {boxE}° W, from {first} to {last}: {m1}, {m2}, {m3} and {m4} ({magType}), none with a depth. USGS: “They were by far the largest east of the Rocky Mountains in the U.S. and Canada.”

stories.title: Alaska, 1964
stories.text: Magnitude {mag} ({magType}) at {time} UTC on {date}, {depth} km deep; the catalog still lists this solution as {status}. USGS: it “is the most powerful recorded earthquake in U.S. history.” In {year} the Alaska map box holds {n} earthquakes of magnitude {floor} or more, {nAfter} of them from that day on.

stories.title: Oklahoma, 2009–2017
stories.text: Magnitude {three} and up between {boxS} and {boxN}° N, {boxW} and {boxE}° W: {c2008} in {y2008}, {cPeak} in {yPeak}, {cLast} in {yLast}. The largest was magnitude {mag} ({magType}) on {date}, {place}. USGS: “The majority of earthquakes in Oklahoma are caused by the industrial practice known as "wastewater disposal".”

stories.title: Kīlauea, 2018
stories.text: From {from} to {to} the catalog lists {n} earthquakes of magnitude {floor} or more on and around the Island of Hawaii. The largest, magnitude {mag} ({magType}) on {date}, was {depth} km deep. USGS: “In 2018, Kīlauea Volcano experienced its largest lower East Rift Zone (LERZ) eruption and caldera collapse in at least 200 years.”

stories.text: Magnitude {m1} ({mt1}) at {t1} UTC on {d1}, then magnitude {m2} ({mt2}) at {t2} UTC on {d2}, {hours} hours later and {depth2} km deep.
